info.name: HackHub
info.description: The REST API of HackHub end to end: the happy path from 00 Setup to 17 Prize payment, and the requests that are meant to be refused in 18 Error handling. Run the folders in order: every request that creates something saves the generated id in a collection variable, so no id has to be typed by hand.

item.name: 00 Setup
item.description: Logs in the development users seeded at startup and stores their ids. These are the actors of every following request.

request.description: Credentials travel in the query string: the endpoint reads them with @RequestParam.

item.name: 01 Auth
item.description: Registration of a brand new user, followed by its login and logout.

exec: pm.test("the response does not expose the password", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json()).to.not.have.property("password"));

request.description: Unlike login and logout, register reads its parameters from the JSON body.

exec: pm.test("the response does not expose the password", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json()).to.not.have.property("password"));

request.description: Uses the id returned by the registration, never a hardcoded one.

item.name: 02 Hackathon
item.description: Creation of a hackathon by organizer1 and update of its information while registrations are still open.

exec: pm.test("the hackathon is open to registrations", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().state).to.eql("REGISTRATION"));

body.raw:
{
    "name": "HackHub Autumn Challenge",
    "rules": "Teams build a working prototype in 48 hours. Only open source libraries are allowed.",
    "location": "Camerino, Polo Informatico",
    "prize": 5000,
    "registrationDeadline": "2026-02-10T23:59:00",
    "startDate": "2026-02-15T09:00:00",
    "endDate": "2026-02-17T18:00:00",
    "maxTeamSize": 4,
    "judgeId": {{judgeId}},
    "mentorIds": [{{mentorId1}}, {{mentorId2}}]
}

request.description: The staff is taken from the ids saved in 00 Setup. The dates respect registrationDeadline <= startDate < endDate, otherwise the creation is rejected, and they sit a couple of weeks after the instant the clock starts from, so that 09 Clock can walk the event through its phases with short jumps.

item.name: Create a hackathon with a staff member already busy

exec: pm.test("the message names who is busy", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().message).to.eql("User already takes part in something else: organizer1"));

body.raw:
{
    "name": "HackHub Spring Challenge",
    "rules": "A second event, refused before it is built.",
    "location": "Camerino, Polo Informatico",
    "prize": 1000,
    "registrationDeadline": "2026-03-10T23:59:00",
    "startDate": "2026-03-15T09:00:00",
    "endDate": "2026-03-17T18:00:00",
    "maxTeamSize": 4,
    "judgeId": {{memberId1}},
    "mentorIds": [{{memberId2}}, {{newUserId}}]
}

request.description: The whole staff is checked before anything is built, and organizer1 is already the Organizer of the hackathon created above: a user takes part in one thing at a time. It runs here and not among the other refusals because the check looks at the participations that are still open, and once the event is concluded the same request would go through.

item.name: Create a hackathon where one user covers two roles

exec: pm.test("the message says what went wrong", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().message).to.eql("Organizer, judge and mentors must be different users"));

body.raw:
{
    "name": "HackHub Winter Challenge",
    "rules": "A second event, refused before it is built.",
    "location": "Camerino, Polo Informatico",
    "prize": 1000,
    "registrationDeadline": "2026-03-10T23:59:00",
    "startDate": "2026-03-15T09:00:00",
    "endDate": "2026-03-17T18:00:00",
    "maxTeamSize": 4,
    "judgeId": {{memberId1}},
    "mentorIds": [{{mentorId1}}, {{mentorId2}}]
}

request.description: The four roles of a hackathon are covered by four different people, and here member1 is asked to be organizer and judge at once. The check works on the identifiers of the request because the one on the active participations cannot see this overlap: when it runs, none of the participations of this hackathon exists yet, so the same user would pass it once for every role.

exec: pm.test("the new name is in the response", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().name).to.eql("HackHub Autumn Challenge 2026"));

body.raw:
{
    "name": "HackHub Autumn Challenge 2026",
    "rules": "Teams build a working prototype in 48 hours. Only open source libraries are allowed, and the repository must be public.",
    "location": "Camerino, Aula Magna",
    "prize": 6000,
    "registrationDeadline": "2026-02-12T23:59:00",
    "startDate": "2026-02-16T09:00:00",
    "endDate": "2026-02-18T18:00:00",
    "maxTeamSize": 5
}

request.description: The staff is not editable here: the body carries only the information proper to the hackathon. The dates move forward by a couple of days, and from here on it is these that decide the phases: the event starts on 2026-02-16, where 09 Clock takes the clock, and ends on 2026-02-18, where 14 Clock takes it.

item.name: 03 Team
item.description: Creation of a team by member1, who becomes its first member.

exec: pm.test("the creator is the first member", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().memberUsernames).to.include("member1"));

request.description: The creator must not take part in anything else yet: member1 is free, while organizer1, judge1 and the mentors are already staff of the hackathon.

item.name: 04 Staff
item.description: Changes to the staff of the hackathon created in 02: a mentor is added and removed, then the judge is replaced. All three requests use member3, one of the users still free at this point.

request.description: member3 is free at this point: organizer1, judge1 and the two mentors are already staff of the hackathon, and member1 is in the team created in 03. member2 is free as well, and joins that team only in 05. The response describes the user who became a mentor, not the participation.
The hackathon has three mentors after the previous request, so member3 is not the last one and can be removed. The response is empty.

It runs after the removal on purpose: member3 becomes free again only once the mentor participation is gone, otherwise the replacement would be refused. The test moves judgeId onto the new judge, so that the variable keeps pointing at whoever judges the hackathon: from here on judge1 is no longer staff of the event.

item.name: 05 Invitations
item.description: member1 invites member2 into the team created in 03, and member2 accepts. A second invitation goes to newcomer, the user registered in 01 Auth, who refuses it: both the answers an invitation can get are covered here. The refusal is the only request of the folder that does not go through TeamFacade. Every other one does, the acceptance above all: it is the request that coordinates the state of the invitation with the membership TeamService creates, which is what a facade is for. The refusal creates no membership and notifies nobody, so InvitationService is the only service it touches and there would be nothing left to coordinate.

exec: pm.test("the invitation is for the team of member1", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().teamName).to.eql("Byte Runners"));

request.description: member1 is the only member of the team, so it is the only user who can invite; member2 is free, as neither 03 nor 04 has used it.

exec: pm.test("the invitation is for the team of member1", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().teamName).to.eql("Byte Runners"));

request.description: newcomer is not the only user free at this point — judge1 is free as well, as the replacement in 04 Staff removed it from the staff and the orphanRemoval on that list deleted its participation along with it — but it is the only one that has taken part in nothing for the whole run: judge1 has been the judge of the hackathon up to 04, member2 is free only until it accepts above, and everybody else is either staff of the hackathon or already in the team. Picking the user with no history at all keeps this invitation independent of what the earlier folders did to the others. It is left unanswered on purpose: it is what the refusal closing the folder answers to.

exec: pm.test("member2 has one invitation, the one sent to newcomer left aside", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json()).to.be.an("array").that.has.lengthOf(1));
pm.test("the invitation comes from the right team", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json()[0].teamName).to.eql("Byte Runners"));

request.description: The list holds the invitations received by member2 and still to be answered, not those sent by a team: this is why the path carries no team id.

An invitation is answered by its recipient only, so the user asking for the acceptance is the same one the invitation is addressed to. Beyond the state of the invitation, the request creates the membership of member2 in the team.

exec: pm.test("the invitation refused is the second one", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().id).to.eql(Number(pm.collectionVariables.get("invitationId2"))));

request.description: The refusal is the other answer an invitation can get, and the only operation that ever writes DECLINED. The path carries a sub-resource because the acceptance already answers PUT on the invitation itself. Unlike the acceptance it does not go through TeamFacade, and it checks no participation of the user: refusing creates no membership, so an invited user who has joined something else in the meantime must still be able to close what is left pending.

item.name: 06 Consultation
item.description: The read-only requests on the hackathons. They run here on purpose: by now the hackathon has been updated in 02 and its staff has changed in 04, so what they return already carries both. The staff of the hackathon is organizer1, member3 as its judge in place of judge1, and mentor1 and mentor2 as its mentors.

exec: pm.test("at least one hackathon is listed", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json()).to.be.an("array").that.is.not.empty);

request.description: The list an authenticated user sees, with the staff of every hackathon. The judge is member3 and not judge1 because 04 replaced it.

exec: pm.test("the hackathon is open to registrations", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json()).to.be.an("array").that.is.not.empty);

request.description: Only the hackathons still in their registration phase. The one created in 02 is there because the clock has not been moved yet: 09 Clock takes the time past its start date, and from that moment on this list would leave it out.

exec: pm.test("the identifier is there, so the visitor can select an event", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json()[0].id).to.eql(Number(pm.collectionVariables.get("hackathonId"))));

request.description: The same hackathons of the first request, converted for a visitor who is not authenticated: the staff is left out, while the information about the event stays. The identifier stays too, because it is what the visitor selects a hackathon with before reading its detail, and it is not reserved information. The two requests differ in the conversion only.
The detail of the hackathon created in 02. mentor1 is still a mentor: 04 added member3 as a further mentor and removed it, leaving the original two untouched.

item.name: 07 Leave team
item.description: It changes the composition of the team, so every folder that counts on the two members left by 05 Invitations runs before it. member2 walks out and member1, who created the team, stays behind as its only member. What runs after works on the team as it is left here: 08 Registration takes part in the hackathon with member1 alone, and the submission and the support request that follow come from that same participation.

request.description: The one who leaves is member2, not member1: member1 created the team and is the only other member, so letting them out would leave the team empty. An empty team with no concluded hackathon behind it is dissolved, and the team the rest of the collection refers to would be gone. The response is empty.

item.name: 08 Registration
item.description: Registers in the hackathon the two teams the event runs on: Byte Runners, with member1 alone as the only member left after 07 Leave team, and Null Pointers, created here by member2. Two participants are needed because 13 Disqualification takes one of them out: with a single team the list of submissions read in 15 Evaluation would come back empty, and an empty list does not tell a filter that works from a hackathon with nothing left in it. The registrationId of Byte Runners is the one submissions, support requests and reports are addressed by, while the second registration is kept apart in registrationId2. The hackathon is still open to registrations. The disqualification used to live here and has been moved to 13 Disqualification, after everything that works on a participating team, because it closes the participation.

exec: pm.test("the team registered is Byte Runners", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().teamName).to.eql("Byte Runners"));

request.description: The hackathon is still in REGISTRATION and its registrationDeadline, moved to 2026-02-12 by the update in 02 Hackathon, is compared with the time of the clock, which still stands at 2026-02-01: an expired deadline would reject the registration. The team is taking part in nothing else and its size fits maxTeamSize. The response carries the registrationId every later operation of the event refers to.

exec: pm.test("the creator is the first member", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().memberUsernames).to.include("member2"));

request.description: The second team is created here and not in 03 Team because member2 belongs to Byte Runners from 05 Invitations until 07 Leave team, and a user already in a team cannot create another one. One member is enough to register, the size of the team is only compared with maxTeamSize.

exec: pm.test("the team registered is Null Pointers", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().teamName).to.eql("Null Pointers"));

request.description: The second team takes part under the same conditions as the first one, with the clock still at 2026-02-01 and the deadline at 2026-02-12. This is the registration that survives the disqualification of Byte Runners and reaches the evaluation.

item.name: 09 Clock
item.description: Moves the time of the platform to the day the hackathon starts. The clock is a development tool, not a use case: the endpoints it holds live under /api/dev and exist only in the dev profile. It runs here because everything before it belongs to a hackathon still open to registrations, and 10, 11 and 12 need an event under way.

request.description: The instant the platform is living in. Right after startup it is the one configured in app.time.fixed, but the value is not asserted: it depends on how many requests have already moved the time, so a run started midway would read something else.

item.name: Move clock to the start of the hackathon

exec: pm.test("the clock is on the day the hackathon starts", () => pm.expect(pm.response.text()).to.have.string("2026-02-16"));

request.description: This is what lets the whole life cycle of a hackathon be walked through in a single run. The phases of an event follow its dates: the hackathon updated in 02 starts on 2026-02-16T09:00, while the clock stands at 2026-02-01, so without this request it would stay in REGISTRATION for the rest of the collection and no submission and no support request could be accepted. The instant chosen is an hour after the start, and the transition is applied the next time a service reads the hackathon.

item.name: 10 Submissions
item.description: The submissions of the two teams, uploaded while the hackathon is under way, and the two ways of reading them back. A submission is accepted only while the event is RUNNING: this folder works because 09 Clock has moved the time past the start date, and the upload is what proves the transition happened. Both teams hand in their work while both are still in the event, so the list read after the two uploads holds two of them.

exec: pm.test("the submission belongs to Byte Runners", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().teamName).to.eql("Byte Runners"));
pm.test("the submission is dated with the time of the clock", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().submissionDate).to.have.string("2026-02-16"));

url.raw: {{baseUrl}}/api/submissions?registrationId={{registrationId}}&title=Byte Runners prototype&description=A working prototype built during the event, with the repository open to the judge.&link=https://github.com/byte-runners/prototype

query.value: A working prototype built during the event, with the repository open to the judge.

request.description: Uploading and updating are the same operation: sending this request again would replace the data of the submission instead of creating a second one, because a team hands in one entry. The submissionDate is not sent by the client, the platform stamps it with its own time: this is why the test expects the day the clock was moved to and not the real one.

exec: pm.test("the submission belongs to Null Pointers", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().teamName).to.eql("Null Pointers"));
pm.test("the submission is not evaluated yet", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().score).to.be.null);

url.raw: {{baseUrl}}/api/submissions?registrationId={{registrationId2}}&title=Null Pointers prototype&description=A prototype built during the event, with the repository open to the judge.&link=https://github.com/null-pointers/prototype

query.value: A prototype built during the event, with the repository open to the judge.

request.description: The work of the team that is not disqualified later on: it is the submission the judge evaluates in 15 Evaluation. Same request as the one above with the other registration, so the id it saves is kept apart in submissionId2.

exec: pm.test("it replaced the entry instead of creating a second one", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().id).to.eql(Number(pm.collectionVariables.get("submissionId"))));
pm.test("the new data is the one that stays", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().title).to.eql("Byte Runners prototype, second version"));
pm.test("the submission still belongs to Byte Runners", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().teamName).to.eql("Byte Runners"));

url.raw: {{baseUrl}}/api/submissions?registrationId={{registrationId}}&title=Byte Runners prototype, second version&description=The same prototype after a last round of work, with the tests the first version was missing.&link=https://github.com/byte-runners/prototype

query.value: The same prototype after a last round of work, with the tests the first version was missing.

request.description: Uploading and updating are the same use case: a team hands in one entry, so a second upload replaces the data of the first instead of creating another submission. The identifier is what proves it, and it is why the request asserts on it: the submission keeps its identity, so whatever is attached to it, an evaluation above all, survives the update. It runs before the two readings, which would otherwise assert on the title of the first version.

exec: pm.test("the list holds the submission of each team", () => {

request.description: Both teams are still in the event here, so both the submissions are listed: this is the state the projection is measured against. The organizer reads them as a member of the staff of this hackathon, which is what the access to this list requires. The submissions of the disqualified teams are left out by the query behind this list, so they never reach the staff; 13 Disqualification runs later, and the very same request repeated in 15 Evaluation comes back with one submission alone.

exec: pm.test("it is the submission uploaded before, with the data of the second upload", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().title).to.eql("Byte Runners prototype, second version"));

request.description: The detail of a single submission, read through the id the upload saved. It is the request the judge opens to look at one entry: the score and the judgment come back null, as nothing has been evaluated yet.

item.name: 11 Support requests
item.description: The support a team asks for while the event is under way, the call a mentor plans in answer to it, and the three ways of reading a request back: the list a mentor works on, the one the team sees, and the detail of a single request. The call sits before the readings on purpose, so that the lists show a request already taken over instead of one still waiting. Like the submissions, this folder works because 09 Clock has moved the time past the start date: support is available only while the hackathon is RUNNING, and the slot of a call has to lie ahead of the clock.

exec: pm.test("the request comes from Byte Runners", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().teamName).to.eql("Byte Runners"));
pm.test("no mentor has taken it over yet", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().status).to.eql("PENDING"));

url.raw: {{baseUrl}}/api/support-requests?registrationId={{registrationId}}&description=The deployment of the prototype fails and we cannot work out why.

query.value: The deployment of the prototype fails and we cannot work out why.

request.description: The request is addressed by the registrationId, not by the team: what asks for support is the participation of a team in an event, so the same team taking part in another hackathon would ask through another registration. It is born PENDING and stays so until a mentor schedules the call it asked for.

exec: pm.test("a mentor has taken the request over", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().status).to.eql("HANDLED"));
pm.test("the request carries the slot just booked", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().callDateTime).to.be.a("string").that.includes("2026-02-16T15:00"));

request.description: The call is planned under the request it answers, because that is where it belongs: a mentor does not open an appointment out of nothing, they take over a team that asked for help. The mentorId is the id of the user who mentors the event, the one the login saved, and the platform looks for it inside the staff of the hackathon: a mentor of another event cannot answer this request. The slot is five hours ahead of the clock that 09 Clock left at 10:00, because a call is planned, not held in the past. The instant is booked here and asked for a second time on purpose at the end of this folder: the calendar is a stub that refuses the same slot for the same people twice, and "Schedule a call on a slot already taken" exists in order to be refused. No other request of the collection may book it. What comes back is the request, not the call: the callDateTime it now carries is the appointment, and the HANDLED status is the request leaving the hands of the mentors.

exec: pm.test("nothing is waiting for a mentor any more", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json()).to.be.an("array").that.is.empty);

request.description: The list a mentor works on holds the requests no one has taken over yet, and it comes back empty: the hackathon has one request only, and the call scheduled above is exactly what takes a request out of the pending state. Run before that call, this same request would have found it waiting.

exec: pm.test("the team sees the request it sent", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json()).to.be.an("array").that.is.not.empty);
pm.test("the request it sent has been handled", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json()[0].status).to.eql("HANDLED"));

request.description: The same requests seen from the other side: this list belongs to the team and holds all of its own, whatever state they are in, while the pending one belongs to the mentors and cuts across the teams of a hackathon. The difference is visible right here: the request the mentors no longer see is still in this list, handled.

exec: pm.test("it is the request sent before", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().id).to.eql(Number(pm.collectionVariables.get("supportRequestId"))));
pm.test("the appointment with the mentor is on it", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().callDateTime).to.include("2026-02-16T15:00"));

request.description: The detail of a single request, read through the id the sending saved. The callDateTime is filled in by now: the call scheduled above is what put it there, and finding it again in a later request shows that the appointment was written to the database, not only returned by the answer that created it.

exec: pm.test("no mentor has taken it over yet", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().status).to.eql("PENDING"));

url.raw: {{baseUrl}}/api/support-requests?registrationId={{registrationId}}&description=The prototype still does not deploy and we would like a second opinion.

query.value: The prototype still does not deploy and we would like a second opinion.

request.description: A second request from the same team, sent only to have a PENDING request for the next call to point at: the first one is already HANDLED, and a call cannot be scheduled twice on the same request. It sits at the end of the folder rather than next to the first one, and the position is a constraint and not a preference: "List pending support requests" asserts that nothing is waiting for a mentor and "List team support requests" reads the first element of the list, so both have to run while this second request does not exist yet. Moving this pair earlier to improve the narrative breaks those two assertions.

item.name: Schedule a call on a slot already taken

exec: pm.test("the message says what went wrong", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().message).to.eql("The calendar has no slot free on 2026-02-16T15:00"));

request.description: The same slot, the same mentor and the same team as the call scheduled above: the calendar stub refuses it, CalendarAdapter turns the refusal into an ExternalServiceException and the platform answers 502 Bad Gateway. This is where the boundary with the external systems shows: the refusal comes from the calendar and not from the platform, and a 500 would have blamed the wrong side. It can only live here, while the hackathon is running: further down the collection the event is concluded and the check on the phase would refuse the call before the calendar is ever asked.

item.name: 12 Reports
item.description: A mentor reports to the organizer a team that violated the rules, and the organizer reads the reports of the hackathon back: the whole list and the detail of a single one. The folder sits between 09 Clock and 14 Clock like the submissions and the support requests, because a report is about behaviour held during the event and is accepted only while the hackathon is RUNNING. It comes before the disqualification on purpose: the report is what the organizer decides upon, so it makes sense that the sanction follows it.

exec: pm.test("the report is about Byte Runners", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().teamName).to.eql("Byte Runners"));
pm.test("the reason is the one sent", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().reason).to.eql("The team used code written by someone outside the hackathon."));

url.raw: {{baseUrl}}/api/reports?registrationId={{registrationId}}&reason=The team used code written by someone outside the hackathon.

query.value: The team used code written by someone outside the hackathon.

request.description: The report does not say who sent it: no parameter identifies the mentor, and the response carries no author. A report is a fact about the team, and the organizer decides on the merit of the violation rather than on who noticed it. The team is addressed by its registrationId, like the support request: what is reported is the participation of a team in an event.

exec: pm.test("the report just sent is there", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json()).to.be.an("array").that.is.not.empty);

request.description: The list the organizer consults, which gathers the reports of the whole hackathon whichever team they are about. An unknown hackathonId comes back as an empty list rather than as an error: the list of a hackathon that collected nothing and the list of one that does not exist look the same from here.

exec: pm.test("it is the report sent before", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().id).to.eql(Number(pm.collectionVariables.get("reportId"))));
pm.test("the reason is the one sent", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().reason).to.eql("The team used code written by someone outside the hackathon."));

request.description: The detail of a single report, read through the id the sending saved. The date comes back as 2026-02-16, the day the clock is living in: the platform stamps the report with the time of its own clock, like the submission of 10 Submissions.

item.name: 13 Disqualification
item.description: It comes after everything that works on a participating team because the disqualification is terminal: once the team is out it can no longer submit anything nor be evaluated. The registrationId it uses is the one saved by 08 Registration and is still valid, because the disqualification marks the registration, it does not remove it.

item.name: Get the teams enrolled in the hackathon

exec: pm.test("no team is disqualified yet", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().every(r => r.state === "REGISTERED")).to.be.true);
pm.test("the registration to disqualify is in the list", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().map(r => r.id)).to.include(Number(pm.collectionVariables.get("registrationId"))));

request.description: The Organizer reads the teams enrolled to choose which one to disqualify: the identifier of the registration comes from here, and it is the same list a Mentor reads before reporting a team. Each entry carries the name of the team and the state of its registration.

item.name: Disqualify a team with no reason

exec: pm.test("the message says what went wrong", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().message).to.eql("Reason of the disqualification is required"));

request.description: The disqualification cannot be revoked and its reason is kept in the history of the event, so an empty motivation is refused. It runs before the disqualification that succeeds because afterwards the registration would already be out and the answer would be 409 instead of 400: RegistrationService checks the state of the event and of the registration first, and only then the reason, since a team that is already disqualified cannot be disqualified again whatever the motivation. The reason travels empty and not omitted: leaving the parameter out altogether is refused by Spring before the service is reached, and that body would carry no message.

The disqualification marks the registration, it does not remove it: afterwards the registration is still there, with state DISQUALIFIED and the reason recorded, and so are the submissions and the history of the event. This is why it is a PUT on the registration and not a DELETE of it. The response is empty.

exec: pm.test("the message says what went wrong", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().message).to.eql("Registration " + pm.collectionVariables.get("registrationId") + " is already disqualified"));

request.description: The team is out already, so the second disqualification collides with the state of the registration: 409 Conflict and not 400, because the request is well formed and it is the resource that is already where the request wants to take it. It proves that checkNotAlreadyDisqualified is there, and it changes nothing: the registration keeps the state and the reason recorded by the request above.

item.name: Get the teams enrolled after the disqualification

exec: pm.test("the disqualified team keeps its place in the list", () => {

request.description: The disqualification marks the registration, it does not remove it: the team stays in the list with its new state, which is what tells the Organizer that the sanction has been applied. The submissions of that team disappear instead from the list the staff reads, because there they are excluded by projection.

item.name: 14 Clock
item.description: The second half of the life cycle: the time moves past the end date and the hackathon closes its doors to the submissions. Together with 09 Clock this folder covers both temporal transitions of the state diagram — REGISTRATION to RUNNING on the start date, RUNNING to EVALUATION on the end date — which are the only ones no one commands: the last one, towards CONCLUDED, is explicit and belongs to the proclamation of the winner. It runs after the disqualification on purpose: moving the phase earlier would change the one 13 Disqualification works in.

item.name: Move clock past the end of the hackathon

exec: pm.test("the clock is past the day the hackathon ends", () => pm.expect(pm.response.text()).to.have.string("2026-02-18"));

request.description: An hour after the end date set by the update in 02 Hackathon. From here on the entries are frozen: a further upload would be refused, because submissions belong to the event in progress.

exec: pm.test("the hackathon has moved on to the evaluation", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().state).to.eql("EVALUATION"));

request.description: The transition is not the effect of the request above: the clock alone changes nothing, and the phase is brought up to date by the first service that loads the hackathon afterwards. This read is that service, which is why the assertion on the state lives here and not on the PUT.

item.name: 15 Evaluation
item.description: The judge expresses himself on the submissions, in the phase the clock reached in 14 Clock. The folder opens by reading the list again, to show what the disqualification changed, then evaluates the entry still in the running and evaluates it a second time: a score is not terminal, the judge can go back on it while the hackathon is being judged, exactly as a team could hand in its work again while the event was running.

exec: pm.test("it is the submission of the team still in the event", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json()[0].teamName).to.eql("Null Pointers"));
pm.test("the submission of the disqualified team is left out", () => {

request.description: The same request as in 10 Submissions, run after 13 Disqualification: there it returned two submissions, here one. The submission of Byte Runners is still in the database and its registration still holds the history of the event, but the query leaves it out. This is the exclusion by projection: nobody chooses to skip that submission, it is never seen. The reader is the organizer here as well, so that the two readings compare like with like: what changed between them is the disqualification, not who is asking.

exec: pm.test("it is the submission that was evaluated", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().id).to.eql(Number(pm.collectionVariables.get("submissionId2"))));
pm.test("the judgment is recorded", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().judgment).to.eql("A working prototype, clean code and a repository anyone can build."));

url.raw: {{baseUrl}}/api/submissions/{{submissionId2}}/evaluation?score=8&judgment=A working prototype, clean code and a repository anyone can build.

query.value: A working prototype, clean code and a repository anyone can build.

request.description: The judge records a score between 0 and 10 and a short judgment. What comes back is the submission and not the evaluation: its projection already carries score and judgment, which came back null when the same submission was read in 10 Submissions.

exec: pm.test("the judgment has been replaced", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().judgment).to.eql("Reviewed after a closer look at the repository: the tests raise the score."));

url.raw: {{baseUrl}}/api/submissions/{{submissionId2}}/evaluation?score=9&judgment=Reviewed after a closer look at the repository: the tests raise the score.

query.value: Reviewed after a closer look at the repository: the tests raise the score.

request.description: Evaluating again replaces the score and the judgment instead of adding a second evaluation: a submission carries one evaluation, and the judge can change his mind while the hackathon is in evaluation. It is the same behaviour as uploading a submission twice in 10 Submissions.

item.name: 16 Proclamation
item.description: The third transition of the state diagram, and the only one somebody commands: the organizer proclaims the winner and the hackathon reaches CONCLUDED. Registering the winner and concluding the event are a single act, because a concluded hackathon with nobody proclaimed is a state the model admits only when there is nothing to choose from. The team proclaimed is Null Pointers, which 13 Disqualification left as the only one in the running and 15 Evaluation as the only one with a score. The phase it reaches is terminal: from here on nothing of the event is modifiable any more, neither a disqualification nor a second evaluation would be accepted. What follows in 17 is not a change of the hackathon but its consequence.

exec: pm.test("the winner is Null Pointers", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().winnerTeamName).to.eql("Null Pointers"));

request.description: The registration proclaimed is the one of Null Pointers, saved by 08 Registration: the winner is looked for among the evaluated submissions, so the registration of Byte Runners would be refused here even though it exists and carries a submission of its own. The two assertions on the response say together what a single request has done: the winning team is recorded and the hackathon is concluded. It is a PUT because it changes the state of a hackathon that is already there, as the disqualification does on a registration. The registrationId is a query parameter and not a body because it names something already existing, and it may be left out only by a hackathon where no submission has been evaluated, which is concluded with no winner at all.

exec: pm.test("the concluded phase holds on reading", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().state).to.eql("CONCLUDED"));
pm.test("the winner is recorded on the hackathon", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().winnerTeamName).to.eql("Null Pointers"));

request.description: The same read as in 14 Clock, with the clock still standing past every date of the event. Reading a hackathon is what brings its phase up to date, so this request runs again the refresh that took the event to RUNNING and then to EVALUATION: here it changes nothing, because the phases only move forward and the concluded one is where they stop. The name of the winning team comes back from the association written by the request above, which is what tells a recorded winner from one that only travelled in a response.

item.name: 17 Prize payment

exec: pm.test("the amount paid is the prize of the hackathon", () => pm.expect(Number(pm.response.json().amount)).to.eql(6000));
pm.test("the payment is dated on the clock of the platform", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().date).to.include("2026-02-18T19:00"));

request.description: The hackathon is the only parameter: which registration gets paid is not a choice of the client but the winner proclaimed in 16, and the amount is the prize of the event, nobody types it in. The path has no identifier of a registration for the same reason the one of Register team has none. The amount asserted is 6000 and not the 5000 the hackathon was created with, because 02 Hackathon updates it while the registrations are still open. The date asserted is the instant 14 Clock left the platform on: it is the proof that the payment is dated on the clock of the platform and not on the real time, which is what lets the whole life cycle be walked through in one run. The response describes the payment recorded, without the identifier of the transaction: that one belongs to the payment system and is kept on the server side, where the log shows it together with the amount converted into cents.

item.description: The prize of the concluded hackathon is transferred to Null Pointers, the team proclaimed in 16. It is the last act of the life cycle and it follows the proclamation because it needs a hackathon already concluded with a winner: before the proclamation there is nobody to pay. The transfer is delegated to the payment system, which is external to the platform and simulated by a stub; what HackHub keeps is the record of the payment, so that the same prize cannot be paid twice. The account credited is the iban Null Pointers was created with in 08 Registration, read here for the first time in the collection.

item.name: 18 Error handling
item.description: The negative cases, in a folder of their own at the very end so that the happy path above can be read without interruptions. Every request here is refused, so none of them changes the state of the platform and the folder can be run again as many times as wanted. It covers four of the five statuses of the error contract: 400, 401, 404 and 409. The 502 lives at the end of 11 Support requests and the two errors of the disqualification in 13 Disqualification, because each of them needs a phase of the event that no longer exists down here. The 500 is not covered at all: it answers an inconsistent state of the stored data, such as a hackathon without an organizer, which no use case of the platform is able to produce. The development clock does produce one on a malformed instant, but it sits outside the model and the collection does not go down that path.

exec: pm.test("the message says what went wrong", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().message).to.eql("The prize of hackathon " + pm.collectionVariables.get("hackathonId") + " has already been paid"));
pm.test("the body carries the five fields of an error", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json()).to.have.all.keys("timestamp", "status", "error", "message", "path"));

request.description: The prize of this hackathon was paid by 17 Prize payment, so paying it again collides with what has already happened: 409 Conflict. The shape of the body is asserted here once for the whole folder, because it is the same for every error the platform answers with.

item.name: Register a username already in use

exec: pm.test("the message says what went wrong", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().message).to.eql("Username already in use: newcomer"));

request.description: The username was taken by 01 Auth. It is not a malformed request, it is a request that violates the uniqueness of the username: 409 Conflict. The user is not created, so running this again answers 409 again.

item.name: Get a hackathon that does not exist

exec: pm.test("the message says what went wrong", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().message).to.eql("Hackathon not found: 999999"));

request.description: A resource that was never created: 404 Not Found, and the message names the identifier that was asked for. Before this feature the same request answered 500 with a body that did not even say what was missing.

item.name: Get a submission that does not exist

exec: pm.test("the message says what went wrong", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().message).to.eql("Submission not found: 999999"));

request.description: The same 404 on a different aggregate, to show that the answer does not depend on which repository was asked: every lookup that finds nothing ends in a NotFoundException.

item.name: Log in with a wrong password

exec: pm.test("the message says what went wrong", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().message).to.eql("Invalid credentials"));

request.description: The user exists and the request is well formed, only the password is not the right one: 401 Unauthorized and not 400, so that a client can tell a wrong password from a malformed parameter. The message stays deliberately vague and does not reveal whether it was the username or the password that did not match.

item.name: Disqualify a team of a concluded hackathon

exec: pm.test("the message says what went wrong", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().message).to.eql("A team cannot be disqualified from a concluded hackathon"));

request.description: The event is over and its winner has been proclaimed, so there is nobody left to exclude from anything: 400 Bad Request. It works on the winning registration, the one 13 Disqualification left untouched, and it leaves it untouched too.

item.name: Submit after the hackathon is over

exec: pm.test("the message says what went wrong", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().message).to.eql("Submissions are accepted only while the hackathon is running"));

url.raw: {{baseUrl}}/api/submissions?registrationId={{registrationId2}}&title=Too late&description=A prototype sent after the event has ended.&link=https://github.com/null-pointers/late

query.value: A prototype sent after the event has ended.

request.description: Submissions are accepted while the hackathon runs, and this one is concluded: 400 Bad Request. Nothing is stored, so the submission of the winning team stays the one that was evaluated.

item.name: Ask for support after the hackathon is over

exec: pm.test("the message says what went wrong", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().message).to.eql("Support is available only while the hackathon is running"));

url.raw: {{baseUrl}}/api/support-requests?registrationId={{registrationId2}}&description=Is there anybody still around to help us?

query.value: Is there anybody still around to help us?

request.description: The mentors answer while the event runs, and this one is over: 400 Bad Request. It is the same rule as the request above, read on a different endpoint.

item.name: Invite into a team you do not belong to

exec: pm.test("the message says the sender is a stranger to that team", () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().message).to.include("is not a member of team"));

request.description: An invitation is sent from inside the team it invites to. member1 belongs to the first team and tries to invite into the second: the membership of the sender and the team of the invitation travel as two separate parameters, so without this check knowing the id of a team would be enough to hand out memberships in a team one does not belong to.
